entry.title: Moving on
entry.content:
Because life is too short to fight technology, and having non-tech hobbies is more fulfilling.

I will move back to GitHub and stop self-hosting.

Thank you Hetzner, Codeberg, etc. It was nice using them.

See you later.

entry.title: Choose your own battle
entry.content:
I don't have much time to spend. I'm not powerful enough to fix all of current world problems. I'm just a young, disillusioned person navigating life.

Hence, I must choose my own battle, since I cannot win all of them at once.

What does this mean in practice?

I can prefer to use free, open source software while still using proprietary Operating System such as Windows or MacOS. I can refrain from using AI in my code while still using AI-affected technologies such as rsync or Linux. I can be easy-going on the outside while still following my compass.

This is not compromising my values. This is prioritising how I value my time.

I don't have much time to deal with computer problems. I don't want to stop using a piece of technology just because it goes against of what I think it should be. I don't want to appear ideological while producing no value.

All in all, it's about being adaptive.

It's sad that I cannot achieve purity and perfection. But what I receive instead will be sanity and time.

And in this burning world, this seems to be the path forward.

Being ideological does have its own benefits, but rejecting reality won't help.

See you.

entry.title: A month of self-hosting
entry.content:
It has been a month since I last bought a cloud server from Hetzner for self-hosting my websites. It's eye-opening experience, and here I am sharing what I've learnt.

Some of these may be unrelated to self-hosting itself, but it's more about experience I gained during last month.

AI bots

They are real and annoying. When I read about them, I didn't fully understand how bad they are, until my server keeps getting traffic from them. I learnt the hard way that as soon as you publish your website to the web, you will see bots. Somehow. And it's hard to tell if there's any real people in that noise.

As far as I can see, these bots mass-scan for endpoints that I don't serve:

I don't use WordPress, nor any CMS. My website is served from a static folder generated by 11ty that is uploaded manually using rsync.

That's suck. These bots mass-scan for vulnerability. I think my server would get compromised very soon if I hadn't properly configured firewall and web server.

I'm not sure why I stopped trying to block them. Perhaps because I'm too tired.

Simplicity

At first, this website is deployed with Coolify. I thought it's a good idea since it provides ease of management, and also the team behind it has a promo-code for Hetzner.

I stopped using it soon after, since I prefer bare-metal experience, and I don't want to deal with the trouble of multi-layered abstraction.

I learnt how to configure Nginx and acme.sh. Although I need to jump around the web to read, it helps me understand.

And it's simpler.

Perhaps that's the point of doing these things manually yourself. It's about understanding and simplicity.

Disillusion

The more I dig deeper into tech, the more disillusioned I am.

Much of the points against AI are already written and I'm not going to repeat them here.

Scope-creep is a real concern. Anything that tries to do too much ends up not doing anything well (I'm looking at you, systemd). Sometimes I look at BSD solutions and I find them to be more sane. I'm even thinking about migrating to BSD for my server.

Obsession of money is the reason why tech has gone shit. Don't get me wrong, it's crucial to make money especially if you are running a business, but I wonder where the line between enough and greediness is.

I'm getting tired of these. Sometimes I wonder if I've chosen the wrong field.

Closing

Well, guess that's most of the experience I gained during last month of managing my own server.

I wonder how this month will go. Guess we'll see and adapt.

See you.

entry.title: Multiple interests
entry.content:
I have a bad habit of dedicating whole day for something I like to do. While I love doing it, it leads me to be exhausted as time goes by.

And eventually, I got burnout. It isn't a good idea after all.

The solution I've found, beside taking breaks, is to have multiple interests and schedule.

For example, beside programming, I can do 3D modeling, reading blogs, managing server I own, writing blogs, thinking, etc.

If I don't feel like doing modeling, I can write a blog, SSH to my server for checking, or sit there and think.

Beside this, having a schedule also helps. I can do programming in the morning, studying English in the afternoon, and pursue my other interests in the evening.

Not only I can maintain my energy every day, but also by having multiple hobbies, it provides a better way to spend my time than watching YouTube or being on social media.

And, it's not like you have to pursue all of your interests in a day. You can span it to multiple.

It's worth giving a try.

This is not about spreading yourself too thin. This is about maintaining your health while having better things to do in your time.

See you.

entry.title: Adapt
entry.content:
What should you do when the unexpected come?

Will you complain? Will you resist? Will you wish that it shouldn't be this way?

No. Being like that won't solve anything.

The only way is to adapt. To be pragmatic.

To be adaptive is to be flexible. In the face of uncertainty, by remaining flexible, you can move forward.

Complaining won't help. Resisting won't help. Wishing won't help either.

What does is being adaptive. Being flexible.

But, do not lose your ideal. Just because you are flexible, doesn't mean you should leave behind your value.

Keep your eyes on the stars, and your feet on the ground.

— Theodore Roosevelt

The stars are your dreams, your values. The ground is reality. By balancing both, you can become who you want to be.

So, be adaptive, while keeping your value.

entry.title: What it means to be human
entry.content:
We fumble, flop, and fail. We make mistakes. We cause trouble.

But, we can learn. We can grow. We can fix them. We can try our best.

It is what makes human unique and beautiful.

Generate AIs cannot be human, no matter how hard we try. Although they also fumble, flop, and fail, they cannot 'learn'. They cannot grow. Because they are, at their core, probabilistic machine.

They are also soulless. Reading a text generated by ChatGPT feels more dull than reading a blog written by a human being.

A text written by a human being has style. It has a soul. It conveys what the writer is thinking. It reflects their experience.

It is what makes a blog worth reading.

Hence, if you use these AIs to write blog for you, then you are not writing. You are generating noise.

To be human is to think. To reflect. To slow down. To be better.

As soon as you start using these AIs, you stop thinking. You stop creating. You start consuming. Just like how social media and news have been enginnering us to.

But, you can do better.

You can start thinking. You can start creating. You can start failing. You can start being better.

You can start being human.

entry.title: Simple tech, simple way, simple life
entry.content:
I like simple tech and simple way of doing things. If a job requires multiple steps with complicated technology, I won't be willing to do it.

Server

For example, I want a way to visualize web server log. I looked at solution like Prometheus and Grafana, and I was like "nah not gonna do this".

...until I saw GoAccess.

I was like "view web server log directly in the terminal? That looks so cool!"

What I needed to do is:

sudo apt install goaccess
sudo goaccess /var/log/caddy/personal-website.access.log --log-format CADDY

That's it. No further setup needed. And it does what I wanted: a way to view web server log visually.

Wanting to keep the dashboard running? Attach a tmux session and run goaccess inside it.

Simple.

Other piece of tech I started using is Caddy. I wanted to have automatic HTTPS without having to deal with certbot and simple configuration syntax.

At first, I hesitate from using it due to it not having rate-limiting feature. It is provided as a 3rd-party module and I need to use xcaddy to compile it.

Well, on the bright side, it provides simple way to configure wildcard certificate for Porkbun.

My Caddyfile is just like this:

{
    acme_dns porkbun {
        api_key {env.PORKBUN_API_KEY}
        api_secret_key {env.PORKBUN_API_SECRET_KEY}
    }
}

(rate_limit) {
    rate_limit {
        zone static {
            match {
                method GET HEAD POST
            }

            key static
            events 10
            window 1s
        }

        log_key
    }
}

islabre.fyi {
    root /srv/Personal-Website
    file_server

    log {
        output file /var/log/caddy/personal-website.access.log
    }

    import rate_limit
}

Also, no more Anubis. I should utilize normal firewall like ufw instead.

Keep it simple.

Website

This website looks simple and barebone. It's my choice. This UI style is applied to many projects I started.

Why? Because it's lightweight and fast. And I don't have to debug my UI often.

If you don't like it, it's fine. I'm not here to please you.

I'm capable of making pretty UI if I'm willing to. I decided to stay simple instead.

Why?

Why stay simple? Why be "boring"? Why?

Because complexity costs everything, from money to my sanity.

And by staying simple, I can be more flexible.

Maybe this resonate with you.

See you.

entry.title: Anubis is now protecting this website
entry.content:
Guess we cannot have peace operating on the web without these bots trying to scrape this website:

I only start this website like a week ago and I have to deal with this!?

Sad.

Anyway, here's now I setup Anubis to help stopping them.

Setup

  1. As always, SSH to the server first:

    ssh personal-server

  2. Install Anubis deb from GitHub:

    curl -fLO https://github.com/TecharoHQ/anubis/releases/download/v1.25.0/anubis_1.25.0_amd64.deb
apt install ./anubis_1.25.0_amd64.deb

  3. Copying default configuration so I could do it for each website I serve:

    cp /etc/anubis/default.env /etc/anubis/personal-website.env
cp /usr/share/doc/anubis/botPolicies.yaml /etc/anubis/personal-website.botPolicies.yaml

  4. Configure /etc/anubis/personal-website.env:

    BIND=:8923
BIND_ADDRESS=tcp
DIFFICULTY=4
METRICS_BIND=:9090
SERVE_ROBOTS_TXT=0
POLICY_FNAME=/etc/anubis/personal-website.botPolicies.yaml
TARGET=http://localhost:7797

  5. Configure /etc/nginx/conf.d/personal-website.conf to use Anubis:

    upstream anubis {
    server localhost:8923;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name islabre.fyi;
    root /var/www/html/Personal-Website;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/islabre.fyi/fullchain.pem; # managed by Certbot
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/islabre.fyi/privkey.pem; # managed by Certbot

    location / {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Http-Version $server_protocol;
        proxy_pass http://anubis;
    }
}

server {
    listen localhost:7797;
    server_name islabre.fyi;
    root /var/www/html/Personal-Website;

    location / {

    }
}

  6. Start Anubis and restart nginx:

    systemctl enable --now anubis@personal-website.service
systemctl restart nginx.service

  7. Visit this website. If you see Anubis splash screen then you're good to go!

UPDATE

It seems that this is not enough. I need to combine Anubis with rate-limiting to stop them from requesting this website too much.

To do it, add the following to /etc/nginx/conf.d/rate-limiting.conf:

limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=1r/s;
limit_req_zone $server_name zone=perserver:10m rate=10r/s;

Update /etc/nginx/conf.d/personal-website.conf:

...
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name islabre.fyi;
    root /var/www/html/Personal-Website;

    ...

    limit_req zone=perip burst=5 nodelay;
    limit_req zone=perserver burst=10;

    ...
}
...

And, test the configuration before reloading:

nginx -t
systemctl restart nginx.service

entry.title: Using certbot for automatic HTTPS
entry.content:
Apparently, Porkbun renews its SSL certificate every 75 days according to their Knowledge Base. This means that I need to download their SSL bundle every now and then.

Since I run my own server, they suggest me to use certbot instead.

This is a tutorial on setting up certbot in case of me forgetting how to do it.

Setup

  1. SSH to the server:

    ssh personal-server

  2. Update the server:

    apt update && apt upgrade

  3. Install certbot and nginx plugin:

    apt install certbot python3-certbot-nginx

  4. Run certbot with nginx option:

    certbot --nginx

entry.title: Setting up this website with Nginx
entry.content:
This is a little tutorial on setting up Nginx to serve this website.

At first, I went with Coolify since it provides me ease of deployment. Later I decided to wipe the server and start over since the tech stack is too complex for my taste, and I want to learn how to set it up myself.

Prerequisites

  • A server that can be SSH'd to (I use Hetzner with Debian 13 installed)
  • A domain (I registered one from Porkbun)
  • SSL Certificate, so this website can be served over HTTPS (Porkbun provides this as a bundle after them setting up SSL for my domain)

Setup

  1. SSH to the server (make sure you set this up first):

    ssh personal-server

  2. Update the server (if required, restart the server using reboot command):

    apt update && apt upgrade

  3. Install nginx:

    apt install nginx

  4. Enable nginx on startup:

    systemctl enable --now nginx

  5. Add the following content to /etc/nginx/conf.d/personal-website.conf:

    server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name islabre.fyi;
    ssl_certificate /etc/ssl/islabre.fyi-ssl-bundle/domain.cert.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/islabre.fyi-ssl-bundle/private.key.pem;

    location / {
        root /var/www/html/Personal-Website;
    }
}

  6. On the host, rsync both the website's build artifact and the SSL bundle to the server:

    cd /path/to/Personal-Website/
npm run build
rsync -av --delete _site/ root@personal-server:/var/www/html/Personal-Website/

    cd /path/to/folder/contain/islabre.fyi-ssl-bundle
rsync -av --delete islabre.fyi-ssl-bundle/ root@personal-server:/etc/ssl/islabre.fyi-ssl-bundle/

  7. On the server, restart nginx:

    systemctl restart nginx

  8. Go to https://islabre.fyi. If the website shows up then you're done!
